## 26. Search rows show the matching lines (2026-11-07)

- **Decision.** Each `search` row gains a `snippet` cell: the lines of the block that matched, numbered, at most three, each cut at 160 characters, with the rest counted. The block's first line is left out when the block has a signature, because that column shows it.
- **Why.** Rows held only a location and a signature, so an agent had to read the file to see why a block matched, a second turn the tool exists to save. Against pinned zustand, zod and axios, the declaration's own line was in the output for 15 of 59 identifiers before and 59 of 59 after (`just rg-compare`); output grew about 1.7x and stays below one `rg -n` call.
- **A rule this replaces.** A test asserted that block code must never appear in rows. That assumed a separate `extract` command that does not exist (its hint was removed with the diagnostics rework), so the rule left agents with nothing to read. The whole block is still not printed; only matching lines are.
- **Rejected.** Printing each block's `code`, as Part 1's snapshot lists: a large block costs more than the question needs, and the budget would have to count printed bytes. A separate `extract` command: a second call for every hit.
- **Open.** `--max-tokens` and `--max-bytes` still count the blocks the printed rows cover, not the snippets printed. Snippets are at most about 500 bytes a row, so the gap is small; counting printed bytes is the follow-up.
## 27. Tokens are estimated, not tokenized (2026-11-08)

- **Decision.** `count_tokens` returns the printed text's byte length divided by three, rounded up, and the `tiktoken-rs` dependency is gone. `--max-tokens` keeps its default of 20,000.
- **Why.** Building the `o200k_base` vocabulary took about 55 ms on the first row of any search with a match, against about 6 ms for the rest of the search: a match cost 50 ms where `rg` costs 9 (zustand, release build). On 15 real outputs from the pinned repos `o200k_base` ran 2.97 to 3.57 bytes per token (mean 3.34), so `ceil(bytes / 3)` reads about 11% high on average and never more than 1% low
- **Also removed.** The 32 KiB byte cap that kept quadratic BPE merging away from minified rows has no purpose without a tokenizer.
- **Rejected.** Keeping the tokenizer and building it on a thread while text search runs: it hides the cost on large repositories only, keeps the dependency and the binary size, and keeps counting with the wrong vocabulary. Rejected: `bytes / 4`, which reads about 17% low on these outputs and so lets a response overspend its cap.
- **Supersedes.** Part 8 §9.1 (byte length as a proven upper bound on tokens) still holds as a bound; the count now uses a tighter ratio and gives up the guarantee that it never understates.
- **Measured.** After the change a match costs about 9 to 11 ms on zustand (was 49), level with `rg -l` in the same run, and 15 queries over the pinned repositories print byte-identical output.

## 28. Budget caps count the printed rows (2026-11-08)

- **Decision.** `--max-tokens` and `--max-bytes` count the text of each printed row (indent included, newline excluded), not the block's code. `apply_budget` takes a `row_text` function; the output layer supplies `search_row_text`. `SearchResponse.total_bytes` and `total_tokens` sum the kept rows.
- **Why.** The agent receives the row, so the cap bounds what it sees. Since §26 a row holds a bounded snippet, so summing whole blocks overstated large blocks and ignored the snippet.
- **Core stays cap-free.** Row rendering stays in the output layer; core only receives the function. Rejected: moving row rendering into the budget module.
- **Rejected.** A tokens-per-byte estimate of the block code: it still measures text nobody prints.
- **Defaults unchanged.** 50 results, 20,000 tokens, 2 MiB.
- **Supersedes.** The open item in §26: the caps now count the snippets printed.
- **Open.** The document header and hints are not counted. The field docs on `SearchResponse` in `types.rs` do not yet say the totals count printed rows.

## 29. Multi-word questions are scored beside identifier lookups (2026-11-08)

- **Decision.** `scripts/rg-compare.questions` lists questions of two to four words, each with an answer file and a top-level symbol, pinned to the shas in `rg-compare.repos`. A question is a hit when the answer file is in monokl's first `--top` (3) files. The gate is `--min-question-recall`, default 0.75. Each row also reports whether the declaration line is in the output and what the `rg` route 
- **Why.** Identifier lookups are where `rg` already wins on cost. The case monokl exists for is the question that takes `rg` several calls, and the script scored none of those.
- **Stale rows fail loudly.** The script re-checks with `rg` that each answer file declares its symbol, so a moved or renamed answer stops the run instead of scoring wrong.
- **Rejected.** Model-judged relevance: it needs model calls and is not deterministic.
- **Open.** Raise the threshold when ranking improves.

## 30. Class-member questions are scored on their own (2026-11-08)

- **Decision.** A question row whose symbol cell is `member:name` names a method, constructor, accessor or arrow-function property declared on an indented line inside a class. The script re-checks that line with `rg` and scores these rows apart from the top-level questions. A hit needs the answer file in the first `--top` files and the member's declaration line in the output. The gate is `--min-me
- **Why.** Top-level questions cannot show whether member blocks help. A separate score keeps the top-level gate unmoved by a change to members, and lets that change be measured against its own rows.
- **Rows.** Eight in zod and eight in axios. zustand has no classes at the pinned sha, so it has none.
- **Open.** The member gate is a floor, not a target; raise it when members become blocks of their own. Closed in §33.

## 31. Members are blocks of their own (2026-11-10)

- **Decision.** A class method, constructor, getter or setter, a class property holding an arrow or function expression, and the same kinds of member in a top-level or exported `const`/`let`/`var` object literal or `export default { ... }`, get a block next to the block that holds them when they span three or more lines. A new `parent` column after `nodeKind` names the holder (`class Foo`, `variab
- **Why.** A query naming a method returned the whole class, so the row neither named nor ranked the member. On the pinned repositories the member questions went from 2 of 16 to 15 of 16 with the declaration line in the output.
- **A match goes to one place.** A hit goes to the innermost block whose own text on that line matches, and to every block on the line when none matches, so a match is never lost. A holder keeps only the hits outside its members and is dropped when it has none. Rejected: giving the hit to the smallest block by line range, which credited a member that only shared the line (`} b() {`, `}, // note`) 
- **Dedup.** A member is exempt only against the holder that strictly encloses it; same-level overlap behaves as before.
- **Not split.** Interface and type members, hooks, members of anonymous classes, `module.exports = { ... }`, nested functions and nested object literals, and members under three lines (found through their holder).
- **Open.** Hooks inside components. The parent of an object member renders as `variable api` because there is no object symbol kind.

## 32. A block whose declared name holds the query words ranks higher (2026-11-10)

- **Decision.** `final_score = round6(bm25 * name * ntype + coverage)`, where `name = 1 + 2 * (query terms found in the declared name / query terms)`. The declared name is the signature, or the first line that is not a comment or decorator, cut at `(`, `<`, `{`, `=` or `:`.
- **Why.** `toJSONSchema` and `safeParse` lost to blocks that repeat a common word. With the bonus, on main, the multi-word questions score 17 of 18 (was 14) and identifier hit@3 58 of 59 (was 56), with output size unchanged.
- **Rejected.** A file-stem bonus alone: it scored 17 of 18 questions but cost member questions (12 of 16). Name plus stem: no gain over name alone.
- **Open.** `export default function X` is classified `other` (weight 0.7), not `function`, which keeps `buildFullPath` and `dispatchRequest` lower than they should be. That is an analyzer defect, not a ranking one.

## 33. The harness gates follow the measured numbers (2026-11-10)

- **Decision.** The defaults are `--min-recall 0.95`, `--min-question-recall 0.9` and `--min-member-recall 0.9`, against 58 of 59 (98.3%), 17 of 18 (94.4%) and 15 of 16 (93.8%) on main. One more miss in any set fails the run.
- **Why.** The old floors (0.9, 0.75, 0.125) were set from the first baselines and sat far below what main now scores, so a regression could pass.
- **Open.** The floors are a ratchet: raise them with the numbers, never lower them to make a change pass.

## 34. A held-out set and a Rust gate join the harness (2026-11-10)

- **Decision.** Three repositories that no ranking change was tuned on (fastify, trpc, date-fns) carry 24 multi-word and 12 member questions, written and checked with `rg` before monokl first ran on them. They score on their own lines (`held-out questions`, `held-out members`) and the Rust rows on the pinned fd checkout pool into one `--min-rust-recall` rate. The three gates default to 0.9.
- **Why.** The declared-name bonus (§32) was tuned and scored on the same 18 questions, so 17 of 18 was optimistic. The held-out set scored 23 of 24 and 12 of 12 on first run, close to the tuned 17 of 18 and 15 of 16, which is evidence the bonus and member rows generalize. Rust scored 22 of 24 (11 of 13 identifiers, 11 of 11 questions, 11 of 11 members) once the analyzer landed.
- **Rule.** Ranking changes may be tuned on the tuned sets and must be reported on the held-out set. A held-out miss is never fixed by editing the question.
- **Open.** The sets are small, so one miss moves a rate by 4 points; read them as a regression guard, not an estimate. The one held-out miss is trpc `create websocket client` (answer file at rank 7).

2c4fd2f4 fix: make the nesting scan sound against the real parsers and fuzz it
Review found three ways the scan could undercount: `for await (` lost its loop head to `await`, a `;` in JSX text reset what the open elements had charged, and each ambiguous `/` rescanned its whole line. All three are fixed, with tests that parse the input in a child process on a small stack to show the hazard is real.

A differential fuzzer now generates nesting-heavy token soups, scans them under a cap scaled to an 8 MiB stack, and parses every accepted input in a child process; an abort is a counterexample. It found more under-estimates, all fixed with regression tests: a template `}` inside a possible regex flipped the backtick parity, Rust 2024 `#"` is a prefix and not a string, unterminated strings, templates, comments and raw strings hid the rest of the source, and the Rust cap let trees deeper than the drop thread holds (now 256 levels).

Claude-Session: https://claude.ai/code/session_01AdtWVgDi4y4qCnpfdozb2n

4836a198 fix: raise the TypeScript nesting cap to 16,384 levels on a 256 MiB parse stack
A component with 3,000 sibling JSX elements has a true depth of about 3 but costs 45,000 units, because closers do not lower the estimate, so the old cap of 4,096 levels rejected it. The cap and the stack grow together by a factor of four, which keeps the margin: the worst nesting at the cap parses in 96 MiB and overflows 64 MiB, so 256 MiB is at least 2.6 times what it needs. End-to-end tests cover sibling JSX, a 12,000-term concatenation and a 20,000-row array.

Claude-Session: https://claude.ai/code/session_01AdtWVgDi4y4qCnpfdozb2n

d07960ae test: cover a file nested past the cap end to end
The nested-file test used 5,000 levels, which is now over the cap, so it is lowered to 1,000. A second test checks that a 100,000-level file is skipped with the depth and cap in the help line while other files are still searched.

Claude-Session: https://claude.ai/code/session_01AdtWVgDi4y4qCnpfdozb2n
Entire-Checkpoint: 01M74HSAK92NYM7AR20WB60HA1

10359c86 fix: parse files on a fixed stack and reject deep nesting before parsing
The parse thread sized its stack by input, so a file's cost and whether it was analyzed depended on its length and on the host's memory. Every parse now runs on one 64 MiB stack, and a linear scan rejects a file whose nesting could pass it before any parser sees it. The size cap is a measured 4 MiB instead of what a stack could hold, and the post-parse tree-depth check and its leaked trees are gone because no accepted tree is deeper than the drop thread holds.

## 23. A parse cannot overflow its stack (2026-11-02)

Resolves [07](./07-edge-cases-and-failure-modes.md) Part 1 #2 and replaces §21's reasoning for the nesting guard.

- **What was wrong.** §21 treated the bracket scan as the bound on the parser's recursion. It is not one. A quote inside a regex literal hid the rest of the file from it, and arrow functions, conditionals, generic types and JSX recurse without brackets. In the release CLI, 5,000 parentheses after `/'/`, 20,000 levels of `Array<`, `() =>` or `a ? b :`, or 30,000 nested `<div>` overflowed the 8 MiB main thread and aborted the whole search with no output. OXC 0.152 has no depth limit of its own.
- **Measured** (parse plus extraction, aarch64 macOS, stack per nesting level, optimized / unoptimized): `(` or `[` 1,562 / 3,241 B; `[` in a type 1,701 / 4,581 B, the most per source byte; `{a:` 1,847 / 3,636 B; `Array<` 1,562 / 3,436 B; `() =>` 802 / 965 B; `a ? b :` 704 / 676 B; `<div>` 464 / 1,218 B; `!` 80 / 561 B. Left-deep `a + b` and `a.b()` chains parse in a loop and cost 80 / 561 B per level only in the extractor's visitor.
- **Choice.** Each file is parsed and extracted on its own scoped thread with 8 MiB plus 4 KiB per source byte (12 KiB unoptimized), over twice the worst measured cost per byte. Every recursion level consumes at least one byte, so no input can overflow it. A file needing more than 1 GiB, longer than 254 KiB optimized or 85 KiB unoptimized, is degraded without parsing. A panic or a thread that cannot start also degrades. `FileAnalysis::degradation` (`TooLarge`, `Panicked`, `ThreadUnavailable`) says which, and the pipeline's `Degraded` diagnostic names it ("file too large to parse (N bytes, over the cap of M)"), so a size skip is no longer reported as a syntax error. A file with syntax errors 
- **Cost.** The worst case is a file at the length limit that nests as deep as its bytes allow: 250,000 `(` or 250,000 `[` after `return /'/` touches 463 MiB of stack and takes 0.13 s (release CLI, one run each, with an ordinary sibling file still returned). Typed or JSX nesting of 20,000 levels stays near the 54 MiB baseline because the parser fails fast. Of 23,222 local TS/JS source files, 131 (0.56%) exceed 254 KiB, nearly all bundler output. A thread per file moved a whole-repo search from 0.11 s to 0.13 s with identical output.
- **The size cap is an accepted trade-off.** A valid, shallow file over the cap loses its results, and the user sees it by name: the diagnostic lists the file path, the byte count and the cap ("1 file degraded: file too large to parse (300000 bytes, over the cap of 260096): src/big.ts"), so the file can be searched with `rg`. About 0.56% of TS/JS files on the maintainer's machine are over the cap, mostly bundler output. Raising the cap later means raising the stack reservation with it.
- **Review findings, and why the scan is gone.** The first version kept the 256-deep scan as an early exit. Review showed it rejects valid files, which is worse than the cost it saves: a quoted string continued over backslash and CRLF ended the string at the line feed, so 257 parentheses inside it rejected the file; after postfix `++` it read division as a regex and skipped the closing brackets, so 256 lines of `values.push(count++ / total);` counted 257 deep. Telling a regex from a division is undecidable for a scan, and the stack already bounds recursion, so the scan and its tests were deleted. A size skip was also indistinguishable from a parse error; it now has its own reason (above).
- **`debug_assertions` stands for "unoptimized".** The per-byte budget is 12 KiB when `cfg!(debug_assertions)` and 4 KiB otherwise, because the unoptimized frames measured above are about 2.7 times larger. The cfg is a proxy: a release profile with debug assertions pays the larger budget and the 85 KiB cap for nothing, and a profile with optimizations off but no debug assertions gets the 4 KiB budget and could overflow on the costliest input. The workspace profiles do not do either today; set the constant by hand if one is added.
- **Rejected.** A scan that bounds recursion on its own: telling a regex from a division, or JSX text from code, needs the parser's context, so a crafted file can always desynchronise the scan, and then nothing bounds the stack. A fixed large stack with the scan as the bound has the same hole. A child process per file survives any overflow but costs a spawn per file and is not available to library callers. `stacker` cannot reach OXC's recursion. A stack proportional to length with no limit lets a 5 MB file reserve about 20 GB and touch about 8 GB.

## 20. Analyzer foundation corrections (2026-10-23)

- **`Ord` on `LanguageId`.** Part 3 §11 keeps a `BTreeSet<LanguageId>` to deduplicate skip diagnostics, but Part 1 §11 derives no `PartialOrd`/`Ord`, so the spec does not compile. `LanguageId` derives both, in declaration order. Rejected: a hash set in Part 3, since both Part 3 and the contract doc 
- **Other departures from Part 1.** `AnalyzerCapabilities` also derives `PartialEq`/`Eq` so analyzers can be tested against expected values. `FileAnalysis` takes `digest: Digest` for `content_hash` (SPEC-011) and records the `profile` it was built under (owner decision: fixed fields per profile, rec
- **For later tracks.** What an analyzer does when `analyze_with_profile` gets a path `supports` rejects is left to the registry track, which checks `supports` first. Part 3's `language_label` matches only 5 of the 13 `LanguageId` variants and will not compile as written.

## 35. Reads, hit lines and run time have stated bounds (2026-11-11)

Follows [ADR 0004](../adr/0004-search-stays-stateless-and-every-stage-has-a-stated-bound.md) rules 2 to 4 (PR 88).

- **Decision.** Text search reads at most 4 MiB of a file (`MAX_FILE_BYTES`), checked on the open handle. A larger file is skipped unread and reported as one grouped line. A hit line is kept to 4096 bytes (`MAX_LINE_BYTES`) and the cut lines are counted in a warning. `--timeout SECONDS` defaults to 30, accepts fractions, and 0 disables it. It is checked between files in text search and between batches in analysis. Each stage always finishes its first batch, so a tiny timeout still returns something. An expired run prints `partial result: ... expired after searching|analyzing N of M files` and exits 0. `tests/scaling.rs` takes the fastest of 5 runs at 2,500 and 10,000 inputs for rank and dedup, text search and a whole search, and asserts the time ratio stays under 10 (a quadratic step gives 16). It never asserts absolute times.
- **Why.** The limit equals the 4 MiB parse cap, so a larger file could only come back as too large to parse after being read whole. On the PR's measurements a directory of forty 5 MB files peaked at 479 MB and one 300 MB line at 752 MB; both are now about 5 MB.
- **Partial results.** They are the only output that differs between runs, because which files are reached depends on speed. A `-term` exclusion applies only to the files reached. Without a timeout, output is deterministic.
- **Cost of the line cap.** A term that matches only past byte 4096 of a line is not seen by required-term and keyword checks. The warning says so.
- **Rejected.** A limit of 8 to 16 MiB: it would read files the analyzers refuse. Absolute-time assertions in the scaling tests: they fail on a busy machine.
- **Open.** The timeout does not interrupt a single file's read or parse; the bound is the 4 MiB limit and the parse stack (36).

## 36. Parse on a fixed stack behind a nesting scan (2026-11-11)

Replaces §23's per-byte stack and its size caps (PR 83).

- **Decision.** Every parse runs on one 256 MiB stack (`PARSE_STACK_BYTES`). A linear scan (`analysis/nesting.rs`) estimates the recursion a file can cause and rejects it before any parser sees it. The cap is 16,384 levels for TypeScript and 256 for Rust. A rejected file is degraded as too deep and named in the diagnostic with its depth and cap. The post-parse tree-depth check and its leaked trees are gone, because no accepted tree is deeper than the drop thread holds. The size cap is 4 MiB (35).
- **Why.** §23's stack grew with the input, so whether a file was analyzed depended on its length and the host's memory. A fixed stack makes cost and outcome a function of the file alone. §23 deleted the scan because it rejected valid files; the scan now errs only upward and is tested against the real parsers.
- **A false rejection, found and fixed.** The first cap (4,096 levels on a 64 MiB stack) rejected a component with 3,000 sibling JSX elements: its true depth is about 3, but closers do not lower the estimate, so it cost about 45,000 units. The cap and the stack grew by 4x together to keep the margin (the worst nesting at the cap needed 96 MiB and overflowed 64 MiB, so 256 MiB is at least 2.6x). End-to-end tests cover 3,000 JSX siblings, a 12,000-term concatenation and a 20,000-row array.
- **Three soundness bugs found by review, fixed.** `for await (` lost its loop head to `await`. A `;` in JSX text reset what the open elements had charged. Each ambiguous `/` rescanned its whole line. Each has a test that parses the input in a child process on a small stack to show the hazard is real.
- **A differential fuzzer.** `soundness_tests.rs` generates nesting-heavy token soups, scans them under a cap scaled to an 8 MiB stack, and parses every accepted input in a child process. An abort is a counterexample. It found more under-estimates, all fixed with regression tests: a template `}` inside a possible regex flipped backtick parity; Rust 2024 `#"` is a prefix, not a string; unterminated strings, templates, comments and raw strings hid the rest of the source; and the Rust cap let trees deeper than the drop thread holds (now 256 levels). On the final code the PR run found no counterexample.
- **Evidence, not proof.** The fuzzer samples inputs; it does not prove the scan never under-estimates. `MONOKL_FUZZ_SECONDS` sets the run length. The estimate stays a deliberate over-estimate wherever the scan cannot tell syntax apart.
- **Rejected.** A child process per file (a spawn per file, unavailable to library callers). A stack that grows with input (the §23 hazard). Raising only the cap, without the stack.
- **Open.** A valid file over the cap loses its results and the user sees it by name.

## 37. Deletions of code nothing reads (2026-11-11)

PRs 84 to 87. Each removed code whose only reader was a test or nothing.

- **Decision.** The query module is crate-private, and tests that scanned source text, probed for absent derives or re-checked exhaustiveness are deleted (PR 84). `coverage_boost` is gone (PR 85): every printed block holds a matching line, so it was a constant 1.0, and `finalScore` is 1.0 lower with the order unchanged. The score breakdown fields and `SearchResponse` totals that only tests read are gone, and `SymbolKind` derives `Ord` instead of mirroring it by hand. `--max-bytes`, `Budget.max_bytes`, the `miette` feature and dependency, and `ToonProjection<N>` are gone (PR 86); `render_search` and `search_row_texts` replace the projection, and `apply_budget` takes the printed row texts. Unread analyzer output is gone (PR 87): symbols, dependencies, exports, JSX, `LangData`, the `Digest` and its `blake3` dependency, `AnalysisProfile`, `AnalyzerCapabilities`, `language_for`, `matched_keywords`, `RankedBlock.parent_context` and `ParentContext.line`. `LanguageAnalyzer` is now `languages`, `supports` and `analyze(path, text)`.
- **Why.** Search reads only `blocks`, `test_blocks`, `had_parse_errors` and `degradation`. `--max-tokens` is `ceil(bytes / 3)`, so the 2 MiB byte cap bound only above about 700,000 tokens. CLI errors render through michi's `DomainError`, so the `miette` derives had no use. Unique crates in the workspace tree went from 252 to 232. PR 87 removed 2,440 lines and added 308, and the release binary went from 3,762,592 to 3,696,240 bytes. Output was byte-identical on 101 queries (87) and on 93 comparisons (86; only `search --help` differs).
- **Consequences.** `--max-bytes` is now a usage error (exit 2). A command that needs a removed field restores it with its analyzer output and a reader. [ADR 0002](../adr/0002-digest-lives-in-monokl-until-wisp-contracts.md) stands for whoever re-adds `Digest`. `LanguageId` keeps `TypeScript` and `Rust`.
- **Rejected.** Keeping the code for a later command: unread code rots and costs build time and review.
- **Open.** The `Language`/`LanguageId` unification. The architecture docs still describe `miette` and `max_bytes`.

## 38. Process lessons (2026-11-11)

- **Decision.** Compile and test the combined state before merging a PR that other PRs touch.
- **Why.** Two merges broke `main` because each PR passed alone. The object-member score tests (PR 70) were written before the name bonus (§32) and failed once both were in. The scaling test constructed a field that a deletion removed (PR 90 fixed it). CI on a branch checks that branch against the `main` it started from, not against what merges beside it.
- **A real race hid behind one runner.** The soundness tests passed under `nextest` (one process per test) and shared one batch file under `cargo test`, where concurrent child launches overwrote each other's file and removed each other's directory. Each batch now has its own directory (PR 89).
- **Rule.** A test suite must pass under both runners. When a PR is stacked or parallel, merge `main` into it and run `just ci` before the user merges.
- **Open.** CI does not yet run `cargo test` beside `nextest`.

- **Rule.** A test suite must pass under both runners. When a PR is stacked or parallel, merge `main` into it and run `just ci` before the user merges.
- **Open.** CI does not yet run `cargo test` beside `nextest`.
